questions.question: If standard NLP benchmarks show nothing unusual, why should we believe GPT-3's meta-learning leap is real?

passages.quote: Nothing in the raw metrics reported on, say, Penn Tree Bank or LAMBADA or WinoGrande would lead you to expect all of this hilarious and creative output

questions.question: If GPT-3 already costs millions of dollars, is scaling it 100-1000x further really economically realistic?

passages.quote: Nonetheless, I think we can expect further scaling. (10×? No, 10× isn’t cool. You know what’s cool? 100–1000×, trained on a fancy new supercomputer.)

questions.question: If the pretraining thesis is logically airtight, why does the author still doubt it will actually work in practice?

passages.quote: The pretraining thesis, while logically impeccable—how is a model supposed to solve all possible trick questions without understanding, just guessing?—never struck me as convincing, an argument admitting neither confutation nor conviction.
Why think pretraining or sequence modeling is not another one of them?

questions.question: If DeepMind has the hardware, budgets, and people, why hasn't it built anything like GPT-3?

passages.quote: They aren’t stupid, they have the hardware, they have the budgets, they have the people.

questions.question: If months after release no other lab has matched GPT-3, does that support or undercut the idea of an oncoming scaling arms race?

passages.quote: A quarter year on from GPT-3 and counting, can you name a single dense model as large as the 17b Turing-NLG—never mind larger than GPT-3?
no model has come near GPT-3, and indeed, no model has even exceeded Turing-NLG’s 17b.

questions.question: Isn't calling GPT-3 'just' pattern-matching or memorization a fair criticism rather than missing the point?

passages.quote: dismiss any model as “just” this or that(“just billions of IF statements” or “just a bunch of multiplications” or “just millions of memorized web pages”)
Showing that some task requiring intelligence can be solved by a well-defined algorithm with no ‘intelligence’ is precisely what success must look like!

questions.question: If training data is just physics, like river hydrology, with no agents in it at all, can agency still emerge from it?

passages.quote: no amount of modeling the chaotic dynamics of Pluto will give you any help in modeling the dynamics of astronomy infighting about whether Pluto is a planet, right?
Humans do, in fact, model natural systems like these as agents. We find such teleological explanations indispensable for intuition and shortcut reasoning across many natural systems.

questions.question: Since capabilities like agency have to 'pay their way' with enough data and scale, couldn't a model simply fail to develop it?

passages.quote: They need rich enough models to compute them feasibly, enough data to force them out of easier solutions (which will fail on a few rare datapoints), and enough training (to work through all the possibilities to converge on the better capabilities).

All you can do is make a complex system that doesn’t display agency as far as you can tell; unfortunately, much like Turing-completeness (or security vulnerabilities), that there is no overt agency doesn’t mean it is not there.

questions.question: If one random Turing machine alone has nothing it's trying to maximize, why would training on many different ones risk producing agency?

passages.quote: There is nothing that random TM programs try to minimize or maximize; they simply run.
This provides our modularity, and a particular computation executed, and strong optimization pressure to rapidly ‘read’ the history and infer what the new rules must be.
